description_full: Hochschild Mining plc, a precious metals company, engages in the exploration, mining, processing, and sale of gold and silver deposits. The company's flagship asset includes the 100% owned Inmaculada gold and silver underground mine consisting of 40 mining concessions covering an area of approximately 20,000 hectare located in the Ayacucho Department, southern Peru. It is also involved in the power generation and transmission activities. It serves in Switzerland, Canada, South Korea, Germany, Chile, Finland, the United States, Luxembourg, Bulgaria, Peru, Brazil, and the United Kingdom. The company was founded in 1911 and is based in London, the United Kingdom.
ceo_bio: Mr. Eduardo Landin Navarro | CEO & Executive Director | Age 55 | Compensation: $1.7M (FY2025)
culture_narrative: Employs approximately 3K people. Revenue per employee of $370K ranks in the bottom quartile among Basic Materials peers. Each employee generates $64K of free cash flow annually. CEO compensation is 5× revenue per employee (modest relative to workforce productivity). Governance score flags low compensation governance risk (2/10).
financial_summary: Hochschild Mining PLC is a mid-cap basic materials business with a $3.3B market cap on $1.2B of annual revenue.

The top line has compounded at +17% over the past three years, the kind of sustained demand persistence that marks a compounder. Operating margins are expanding by +7.6pp year-over-year, which is one of the strongest signals that the moat is deepening.
Returns on capital run at 13% against a 9% cost of capital, a 4-point spread that creates value, though narrow enough that competitive pressure could close it, with gross margins sitting at 32%.

The business throws off $206M in free cash flow — roughly 17 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 2.10× so those profits are backed by real cash.
Accruals are elevated at -10.3% of assets, and Sloan showed firms building earnings through accruals rather than cash systematically underperform.
On the balance sheet, leverage is comfortably conservative at 0.1× net debt/EBITDA, and interest coverage of 16× is fortress-like.

Shareholder yield is only 0.5%, a thin return of capital, and insiders hold 38% of the shares, so management thinks like owners because it is one — the strongest alignment there is, and within its sector the business captures 2.2× its fair share of profits, a structural advantage visible in the numbers.

sector_headwinds.text: Volatile returns on capital suggest the moat is narrower than a snapshot ROIC implies
Above-average SGA growth (16% YoY) warrants monitoring
Cyclical sectors like Basic Materials tend to underperform in slowdowns
Late-cycle dynamics increase the probability of a slowdown
Commodity price volatility and cost-curve position — in a downturn only the lowest-cost producer has a business, and the rest carry the overhead.
Environmental remediation liability — tightening regulations on emissions, tailings, and water use create open-ended balance-sheet risk that grows with each legislative cycle.
Trade policy and tariff whiplash — materials producers are first-order casualties of protectionist swings, and margin gets squeezed from both input and output pricing.

sect: Its 29% operating margin runs 20pp above the Basic Materials median (10%), a real cost or pricing edge over peers.
It captures 2.23x its revenue share in sector profits, taking a disproportionate slice of the profit pool.
The sector is fragmented and competitive (HHI 0.04 across 219 companies in the universe; the top four hold 25% of revenue), so pricing power is hard to come by.
mkt: The shares are in a strong uptrend, up 57% over the past year excluding the latest month.
The price sits mid-way through its 52-week range, 43% below the high.
With annualised volatility of 67% and a beta of 1.05, it moves roughly with the market, though its beta has shifted (1y 2.18 vs 5y 1.11), so read it loosely.
Trading is thin (about $17K a day), below the $1.0M liquidity floor flagged; building a position would move the price.
In past sell-offs it fell 56% in the 2020 crash and 70% in the 2022 bear market.
val: The stock trades 60% below its DCF fair value of $16.07, a meaningful margin of safety.
The fair-value models disagree (dispersion 37%), and the Monte Carlo range runs $6.60 to $37.49 (P10-P90), so treat the estimate as noisy.
On multiples it looks cheap against Basic Materials peers: P/E 11.1 vs 16.5, EV/EBITDA 4.1 vs 8.5 and P/FCF 16.1 vs 22.8 (sector median).
Earnings yields are attractive: an FCF yield of 6.2% (above the risk-free rate) and an EBIT/EV of 10.1% (vs the 8% bar).
The price implies 9.0% annual cash-flow growth, 16pp less than the model expects.
prof: ROIC of 13% earns above the cost of capital of 9.4%, but the 4pp spread is short of the 7pp moat bar; returns have swung a lot from year to year (CV 0.76).
It runs a 32% gross margin and converts 17% of revenue into free cash flow.
Earnings quality is mixed: a Piotroski score of 8/9 and cash conversion of 2.10x, but high accruals (-10.3% of assets).
ROE of 28% comes mostly from margins and asset turnover rather than leverage (3.0x equity multiplier).
SG&A jumped 16% last year, worth watching.
hlth: Leverage is conservative at 0.1x net debt to EBITDA ($319.6M of cash against $348.6M of debt), with interest covered 15.8x.
No distress or manipulation flags (Altman Z 3.4, in the safe zone).
The current ratio of 0.99 means short-term liabilities exceed current assets.
The Beneish M-score (-1.88) sits just under the manipulation line, so earnings quality bears watching.
growth: Revenue has compounded at 17.1% over 3 years.
At current returns, reinvesting 72% of profits supports about 9.7% a year of fundamental growth, enough to sustain growth.
own: Insiders own 38.4%, meaningful skin in the game, and institutions hold 45%.
Shareholder yield is a modest 0.5% (1.4% in dividends).
people: With about 3,199 employees, each generates about $370K of revenue, 0.6x the Basic Materials median.
That works out to $64K of free cash flow per employee.
CEO pay is $1.7M (5x revenue per employee), and compensation governance scores well (2/10, lower is better).
